guide.summary: Thermodynamics connects the microscopic motion of particles to macroscopic quantities such as pressure and temperature, and tracks energy transfer as heat and work. You must use the ideal gas law, kinetic theory, the first law (ΔU = Q + W with W done on the gas), PV diagrams, thermal conduction, and the second law.

sections.heading: Kinetic theory and the ideal gas law
sections.body: Gas pressure results from particles colliding with container walls: P = F/A. Temperature (in kelvins) is proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of particles: K_avg = (3/2)k_BT. At the same temperature, all ideal gases have the same average kinetic energy, so lighter particles move faster (v_rms ∝ √(T/m)). Ideal gas law: PV = nRT = Nk_BT. Doubling absolute temperature at constant volume doubles pressure; doubling volume at constant temperature halves pressure.

sections.heading: First law and PV diagrams
sections.body: Internal energy U of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. First law (AP convention): ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the gas and W is work done on the gas, W = −PΔV for constant pressure. On a PV diagram, the area under a curve equals the magnitude of work; expansion means the gas does positive work (W on gas negative). Processes: isobaric (constant P), isochoric/isovolumetric (constant V, W = 0, ΔU = Q), isothermal (constant T, ΔU = 0, Q = −W), adiabatic (Q = 0, ΔU = W). For a closed cycle, ΔU = 0; the net work equals the enclosed area; a clockwise cycle (P vertical, V horizontal) means net work done by the gas is positive and net heat flows in.

sections.heading: Heat transfer and the second law
sections.body: Thermal energy transfers by conduction, convection, and radiation, from higher to lower temperature until thermal equilibrium. Rate of conduction: Q/Δt = kAΔT/L, increasing with conductivity, area, and temperature difference and decreasing with thickness. Specific heat: Q = mcΔT. The second law: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases; heat flows spontaneously only from hot to cold, and no heat engine is 100% efficient.

keyTakeaways: ΔU = Q + W, W = work on the gas.
Isothermal: ΔU = 0; adiabatic: Q = 0; isochoric: W = 0.
Cycle: ΔU = 0, net W = enclosed area.
commonMistakes: Sign errors from using work done by the gas in ΔU = Q + W.
Saying temperature measures total energy rather than average kinetic energy.
Forgetting that heat added during an isothermal expansion all becomes work.
examTips: PV diagram questions: find T at points using PV ∝ T.
State the sign of Q, W, and ΔU for each process with reasons.
Microscopic explanations: refer to collision frequency and force per collision.
Conduction questions test proportional reasoning with k, A, ΔT, L.
guide.cramSheet:
**Kinetic:** K_avg = (3/2)k_BT · v_rms ∝ √(T/m)

**Gas:** PV = nRT = Nk_BT · T in K

**First law:** ΔU = Q + W (W on gas = −PΔV)

**Processes:** isobaric · isochoric (W = 0) · isothermal (ΔU = 0) · adiabatic (Q = 0)

**Cycle:** ΔU = 0 · net W = area · clockwise → net work by gas > 0

**Conduction:** Q/Δt = kAΔT/L

**2nd law:** entropy of isolated system ≥ 0 change · heat flows hot → cold

vocab.definition: The total kinetic and potential energy of particles in a system; for an ideal gas, depends only on temperature.
PV = nRT, relating pressure, volume, amount, and absolute temperature of an ideal gas.
A process at constant volume; no work is done.
A process at constant temperature; internal energy is constant.
A process with no heat transfer.
ΔU = Q + W; energy is conserved for a thermodynamic system.
A material property describing how well it conducts heat.
The state in which objects in contact have the same temperature and no net heat flows.
A measure of the number of microscopic arrangements; never decreases for an isolated system.
A measure of typical particle speed in a gas, proportional to √(T/m).
Energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K.

practice.topic: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure
practice.stem: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is doubled. The average translational kinetic energy of its molecules

distractors.C: That's the change in rms speed.

practice.stem: Two moles of an ideal gas at 300 K occupy 0.050 m³. What is the pressure? (R = 8.31 J/mol·K)
During an adiabatic compression of an ideal gas, which is true?

choices.text: Q = 0, work is done on the gas, and the temperature increases.

practice.explanation: With Q = 0, ΔU = W > 0, so internal energy and temperature rise.

practice.stem: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been sitting in the same room for hours. The metal spoon feels colder to the touch because

choices.text: the metal spoon is at a lower temperature
metal has a higher thermal conductivity, so it transfers energy away from your hand faster

practice.explanation: Both are at room temperature; the metal conducts heat from your skin faster.

distractors.A: They are in thermal equilibrium with the room.

practice.stem: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 0.010 m³ to 0.030 m³ while 10,000 J of heat is added. What is the change in internal energy?

distractors.A: Adds the work with the wrong sign.

practice.topic: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure
practice.stem: Helium (4 g/mol) and argon (40 g/mol) are in thermal equilibrium. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Helium atoms have 10 times the rms speed of argon atoms.
Argon atoms have greater average kinetic energy.
Both have the same rms speed.
The atoms have the same average kinetic energy, and helium atoms have a higher rms speed.

practice.explanation: Same T → same K_avg; v_rms ∝ 1/√m, so helium is √10 ≈ 3.2 times faster.

practice.stem: An ideal gas expands isothermally. Which describes heat and work?

choices.text: Heat flows into the gas, equal in magnitude to the work the gas does.
Heat flows out of the gas.

practice.explanation: ΔU = 0, so Q = −W; the gas does work, so heat must enter.

practice.stem: A wall has thermal conductivity 0.80 W/(m·K), area 2.0 m², and thickness 0.10 m. The inside is 20 K warmer than outside. What is the rate of heat conduction?
A sealed rigid container of gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. The pressure

choices.text: increases by a factor of about 12

practice.explanation: 300 K → 600 K at constant V doubles P.

practice.topic: Kinetic Theory of Temperature and Pressure
practice.stem: At constant temperature, the volume of a gas is halved. From a microscopic perspective, why does pressure double?

choices.text: Each collision exerts twice the force.
Molecules collide with each unit area of wall twice as often, with the same average force per collision.

practice.explanation: Same speeds (same T) but higher number density means more frequent collisions.

distractors.A: Speed depends on T, which is constant.

practice.stimulus: A gas is taken around a closed cycle that traces a clockwise loop on a PV diagram (pressure on the vertical axis), enclosing an area of 500 J.
practice.stem: Over one complete cycle, which is correct?

choices.text: ΔU = 0; 500 J of net work is done on the gas; 500 J of heat flows out.
ΔU = 0; the gas does 500 J of net work; 500 J of net heat flows into the gas.

practice.explanation: Returning to the initial state gives ΔU = 0. Clockwise means net expansion work by the gas; Q_net = −W_on = 500 J.

practice.stem: A gas goes from state A to state B by two paths. Path 1: isobaric expansion then isochoric pressure drop. Path 2: isochoric pressure drop then isobaric expansion. Which statement is true?

choices.text: Both paths involve the same work and heat.
ΔU is the same for both paths, but the gas does more work along path 1, so more heat is added along path 1.
More work is done along path 2.

practice.explanation: U is a state function. Path 1 expands at the higher pressure, so the area under it (work by gas) is larger.

practice.topic: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
practice.stem: A hot block and a cold block are placed in contact inside an insulated box until they reach equilibrium. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The total entropy of the two blocks increases.
The total entropy decreases because the system becomes more uniform.
The entropy of the hot block increases.

practice.explanation: Spontaneous heat flow from hot to cold in an isolated system increases total entropy.

distractors.C: The hot block loses energy; its entropy decreases (less than the cold block's increase).

practice.stem: Container X holds gas at pressure P, volume V, temperature T. Container Y holds the same type of gas at pressure 2P, volume V/2, temperature 2T. How does the number of molecules in Y compare with X?

choices.text: Y has four times as many.

practice.explanation: N = PV/(k_BT): (2P)(V/2)/(2T) = PV/(2T), half of X's.

practice.prompt: A sample of ideal gas undergoes a cycle. State A: P = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, V = 0.010 m³. The gas expands at constant pressure to state B (V = 0.030 m³), then its pressure drops at constant volume to state C (P = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), then it returns to A along a straight line on the PV diagram.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Starting from a fundamental relationship, calculate the work done by the gas from A to B.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Identify the state (A, B, or C) with the highest temperature and justify.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done by the gas over one complete cycle, and determine the net heat added to the gas.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: For process B → C, determine whether heat flows into or out of the gas. Justify using the first law.

rubric.description: Uses PV = nRT with n constant, so T ∝ PV.
State B, because PV is largest there (9,000 J vs 3,000 J at A and C).
Net work equals enclosed triangular area.
½(0.020)(2.0 × 10⁵) = 2,000 J by the gas (clockwise cycle).
ΔU = 0 for a cycle, so Q_net = 2,000 J into the gas.
W = 0 (constant volume) and T decreases, so ΔU < 0.
Q = ΔU < 0: heat flows out of the gas.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. The work done by the gas at constant pressure is W_by = PΔV = (3.0 × 10⁵ Pa)(0.030 − 0.010 m³) = 6,000 J.

B. From PV = nRT with n constant, T is proportional to PV. T_B/T_A = (P_BV_B)/(P_AV_A) = (3.0 × 10⁵)(0.030)/[(3.0 × 10⁵)(0.010)] = 3.

C. State B has the highest temperature, because the product PV is greatest there: 9,000 J compared with 3,000 J at both A and C.

D. The net work over the cycle equals the area enclosed on the PV diagram, a right triangle with base 0.020 m³ and height 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa: ½(0.020)(2.0 × 10⁵) = 2,000 J. Because the cycle is clockwise, this is net work done by the gas. Over a full cycle ΔU = 0, so ΔU = Q + W_on gives Q = −W_on = +2,000 J: 2,000 J of net heat is added to the gas.

E. From B to C the volume is constant, so W = 0. Pressure drops at constant volume, so temperature decreases and ΔU < 0. Since ΔU = Q + W = Q, Q is negative: heat flows out of the gas.
